title: Mysterious lights illuminate California sky, ambitious project to turn night into day revealed
excerpt: Mysterious lights illuminate California sky, ambitious project to turn night into day revealed
content:
mystery

Express newspaper

01/11/2026 11:51

Two extremely powerful beams of light, appearing in the sky of the California desert, have surprised residents and drivers. Behind the phenomenon that initially seemed inexplicable is an American technology company, which intends to place thousands of mirrors in Earth's orbit to reflect the light of the Sun at night. The project has aroused interest, but also serious concerns among astronomers and environmental organizations.

Residents of the small town of Lone Pine, near Mount Whitney in California, were treated to an unusual sight after two powerful beams of light illuminated the desert sky on Saturday night.

The lights were so intense that they caught the attention of drivers traveling along Highway 395, some of whom stopped to discover their source.

Cayden Thompson, one of the witnesses, told the San Francisco Chronicle that the light was blinding and bore no resemblance to normal vehicle lighting.

"They produced so much energy that you couldn't stand in front of them without risking getting burned. It was incredible," he declared.

However, the explanation for the phenomenon was almost as unusual as the sight itself.

Behind the lights was the American company Reflect Orbital, which is developing a technology to reflect sunlight from space towards the Earth's surface.

A project to illuminate the Earth at night

Reflect Orbital, based in Hawthorne, California, aims to build a network of 50 satellites equipped with large mirrors.

The idea is to place mirrors in orbit and reflect the Sun's light towards areas of Earth where it is night.

The company describes this concept as an on-demand lighting service.

In theory, the technology could be used to supply light to solar plants after sunset, to illuminate urban areas, or to assist search and rescue teams during night operations.

If realized, the system would represent a completely new way of using solar energy.

However, the project is still in the development and testing phase, and its feasibility and large-scale impacts remain to be assessed.

What happened in the California desert?

According to the company, the mysterious lights seen near Lone Pine were part of a controlled experiment.

Reflect Orbital had placed two high-powered ground reflectors on a work vehicle in the area of ​​Horseshoe Meadows Road.

The goal was to simulate the lighting that the company hopes to provide in the future through orbital mirrors.

The volunteer organization China Lake Mountain Rescue, which specializes in search and rescue operations in difficult terrain, participated in the experiment.

The teams conducted search exercises, transporting the injured on stretchers, and preparing equipment, initially in the dark with the help of personal lamps and then under the lighting of the company's floodlights.

The difference was obvious.

Phillip Cash, the organization's chief operating officer, said the illumination was more powerful than what a full moon usually provides.

"At first there's no light and then, suddenly, you can see almost five kilometers around, in every direction," he explained.

According to him, the powerful lighting made it easier to carry out rescue tasks.

The company stressed that the test was conducted with the appropriate permits and in coordination with local authorities, police and Edwards Air Force Base.

"Search and rescue teams are expected to be our first customers. Therefore, this was a real-world test with people who can use our technology," Reflect Orbital said.

Giant mirror 650 kilometers above Earth

The company's plans go far beyond the use of ground-based reflectors.

Reflect Orbital has announced that it has secured two rocket launches through Indian space technology company Skyroot Aerospace.

The objective is to test the Eärendil-1 satellite, which is expected to be equipped with a mirror with a diameter of about 18 meters.

The satellite would be placed at an altitude of approximately 640 kilometers above the Earth's surface.

The mirror would aim to reflect sunlight towards a circular area with a diameter of approximately 4,8 kilometers.

According to the company's concept, a person observing the satellite from Earth could see it as a bright point in the sky, with brightness comparable to the full Moon or the planet Venus.

Reflect Orbital aims to create a network of 50 satellites by 2035.

The company estimates that the lighting service will cost around £3.700 per hour for light reflected from a mirror, depending on the terms of the contract.

These are stated objectives of the company and not capabilities that have already been demonstrated by a functional orbital system.

Astronomers warn of light pollution from space

Despite the technology's potential, the project has faced criticism from astronomers and organizations that protect the night sky.

The main concern is related to light pollution, which can affect astronomical observations and the natural environment.

Ruskin Hartley, executive director of the nonprofit organization DarkSky, called the idea a particularly problematic form of light pollution.

"This is light pollution from space and it is the worst form of it. You cannot turn it off, block it or decide about it through local authorities," he declared.

Hartley also criticized the way the experiment was organized in California, claiming that local astronomers were not informed in advance.

According to him, the demonstration showed that rescue teams can work in conditions similar to moonlight, a phenomenon that nature provides periodically at no cost.

He warned that a technology tested today over California could be used tomorrow to illuminate other areas of the world, including natural spaces that currently have relatively dark skies.

"Would we really want our homes to be lit from space?"

Even Dr. Robert Massey, deputy executive director of the Royal Astronomical Society in the United Kingdom, has expressed concerns about the project.

He described the concept as a potential source of light pollution from space.

"I'm not at all surprised that the experiment has caused so much criticism," Massey said.

He also raised a question about the potential impact of technology on everyday life.

"Would we really want, in the future, rays of light from space to illuminate our homes and workplaces in this way?" he asked.

Astronomers fear that orbital mirrors could create interference during telescope observations and hinder the study of distant celestial objects.

Furthermore, a network of tens of thousands of satellites would raise further questions about orbit management and the impact on space activities.

Concerns also for animals and ecosystems

The criticisms are not limited to astronomy.

Environmental organizations warn that artificial lighting at night can affect the biological rhythms of animals.

Many species rely on the natural day-night cycle to determine the timing of feeding, reproduction, migration, and rest.

Sudden changes in light levels can cause disorientation or behavioral changes, especially in organisms that are active at night.

For this reason, experts require that any such project be carefully assessed for potential ecological impacts.

Company defends project: It could help save lives

Reflect Orbital rejects the idea that its technology should be seen solely as a source of pollution.

According to the company, orbital mirrors can help reduce the use of fossil fuels by expanding the possibility of harnessing solar energy.

She emphasizes that she is collaborating with astronomers and scientists to develop the project and examine the potential impacts.

The company also promises to continue coordinating with communities and authorities in the areas where it conducts its activities.

"We will continue to work closely with communities and local authorities wherever we operate and are excited to show how this technology can help save lives," Reflect Orbital said in a statement.

Could this technology change the way we use light?

The Reflect Orbital project presents an ambitious idea: using mirrors in space to send sunlight to Earth even after sunset.

If the technology proves viable, it could create new opportunities for emergency operations and some uses of solar energy.

However, important questions about efficacy, cost, safety and environmental impact still remain unanswered.

The mysterious lights over the California desert turned out to be part of a technological experiment, but they have opened a wider debate: how far should human intervention in the natural environment go to exploit new sources of energy and lighting? /GazetaExpress/
